questions.q:
Riya grinds a piece of chalk with a mortar and pestle and looks at the powder through a magnifying glass. She says, 'These tiny white grains I can see must be the constituent particles of chalk.'
(a) What kind of change is grinding, and what does that tell you about each grain she sees?
(b) Using (a) and one more fact from the chapter, explain why her grains cannot be the constituent particles.
questions.a: (a) Grinding is a physical change: no new substance is formed, so each grain is still a speck of chalk, only smaller. (b) Since each grain is still chalk and can be ground further, it is not the smallest unit. Constituent particles are so small that they cannot be seen even through an ordinary microscope, so a grain visible through a magnifying glass must itself be made of a very large number of constituent particles.
s: (a) grinding is a physical change, so each grain is still chalk, only smaller
(b) grain can be broken further and constituent particles cannot be seen even through an ordinary microscope, so the grain is made of many of them

questions.q: Kabir looks at a speck of chalk powder through his school's ordinary microscope. It still looks like a solid lump of chalk with no gaps or separate units in it. What is the best way to explain this?
questions.a: Its constituent particles are too small for that microscope
o: Its constituent particles are too small for that microscope
Chalk is one continuous solid and has no particles in it
Grinding has fused all of its particles into one large lump
The speck is itself one single constituent particle of chalk

questions.q:
A Class 8 group in Pune did two activities under their teacher's supervision and wrote this record.
Step 1: Broke a chalk stick by hand again and again until the bits were too small to break. Note: every bit is still chalk.
Step 2: Ground the bits in a mortar and looked through a magnifying glass. Conclusion written: 'Grinding has turned the chalk into its constituent particles, and now we can see them.'
Step 3: Put two teaspoons of sugar in a glass of water, did not stir, tasted the top layer. Note: not sweet.
Step 4: Stirred until no sugar could be seen, tasted the top layer. Note: sweet. Conclusion written: 'The sugar has been destroyed, so the sweetness must come from a new substance.'
(a) Explain why the top layer tasted sweet in Step 4 but not in Step 3.
(b) Find the error in the conclusion of Step 2 and correct it.
(c) Find the error in the conclusion of Step 4 and correct it.
(d) Write one corrected conclusion about matter that Steps 2 and 4 together support, and say what each step adds to it.
questions.a: (a) Without stirring, the sugar stayed mostly undissolved, so its particles had not spread into the top layer. Stirring dissolved it completely: the sugar broke into its constituent particles, which spread through the water into the spaces between water particles, so every layer, including the top, tasted sweet. (b) The specks seen through a magnifying glass are still chalk and can be broken further; constituent particles are so small that they cannot be seen even through an ordinary microscope, so the group is seeing tiny specks, each made of a very large number of constituent particles. (c) The sugar is not destroyed and no new substance forms: it is still present, as the sweet taste shows; it has broken up into its constituent particles, which are too small to see. (d) Matter is made of a very large number of extremely small constituent particles that cannot be seen. Step 2 shows that a substance can be broken into smaller and smaller pieces that are still the same substance; Step 4 shows that a substance can break up into particles too small to see whose presence can still be sensed (by taste).
s: (a) unstirred sugar had not dissolved; stirring broke it into constituent particles that spread through all the water
(b) visible specks are still chalk; constituent particles cannot be seen even through an ordinary microscope
(c) sugar is still present as invisible constituent particles, shown by the taste; no new substance
(d) conclusion that matter is made of extremely small particles, with what Step 2 and Step 4 each contribute

questions.q:
Consider these statements about the particles that make up matter.
Statement 1: Grains of sand on a riverbank are the smallest units into which a rock can be broken.
Statement 2: A speck of chalk too small to break by hand is still made of a very large number of constituent particles.
Statement 3: Once sugar has dissolved, its constituent particles can be seen with an ordinary microscope.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 only
o: 2 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: Aman explains dissolving to his younger sister: 'When sugar disappears in water, it breaks up into its constituent particles, and these particles push the water particles apart to make room for themselves.' Is Aman right? Judge each half of his explanation.
questions.a: Partly right. The first half is correct: dissolved sugar breaks up into its constituent particles, which cannot be seen but can be sensed by taste. The second half is wrong: the sugar particles do not push water particles apart to make new room; there are already spaces between the water particles (interparticle spaces), and the sugar particles separate and occupy these available spaces.
s: verdict: partly right
first half correct: sugar breaks into invisible constituent particles
second half corrected: particles occupy the existing interparticle spaces between water particles

questions.q: At room temperature, three substances A, B and C are a solid, a liquid and a gas, but not necessarily in that order. The attraction between particles is strongest in A, a little weaker in B and weakest in C. Using the idea that the strength of this attraction decides the state, the gas is substance ___. (Write the letter.)
questions.a: C

questions.q:
Ishaan wrote three lines in his notebook after the chalk and sugar activities.
Line 1: 'The constituent particles of chalk can be seen with a good magnifying glass once it is ground finely.'
Line 2: 'Chalk, sand and clay are each made of a very large number of constituent particles.'
Line 3: 'How strongly particles attract each other depends only on how far apart they are.'
Find the two wrong lines, correct each one, and say which line is right.
questions.a: Line 1 is wrong: constituent particles are so small that they cannot be seen even through an ordinary microscope; the specks seen through a magnifying glass are still chalk, each made of very many particles. Line 3 is wrong: the strength of interparticle attraction depends on the nature of the substance as well as on the distance between the particles. Line 2 is right: like chalk, the grains of sand and clay are not the smallest units; each is made of a large number of its constituent particles.
s: Line 1 corrected: particles cannot be seen even through an ordinary microscope
Line 3 corrected: strength also depends on the nature of the substance
Line 2 identified as right, with the reason

questions.q: Which of these would the chapter call a constituent particle of sugar?
questions.a: A unit of sugar that cannot be broken any further
o: A unit of sugar that cannot be broken any further
One single grain of sugar taken from the packet
A tiny speck of sugar dust floating in sunlight
Half of one grain after it is crushed in a mortar

questions.q: True or false? 'If a lump of chalk and its finely ground powder are compared, the powder is made of smaller constituent particles than the lump.' Give your verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. Grinding is a physical change that only reduces the size of each speck of chalk. Every speck, however fine, is still chalk and is made of the same constituent particles as the lump; only the number of particles in each piece is smaller.
s: verdict: false
reason: grinding only makes specks smaller; the constituent particles are the same in lump and powder

questions.q:
Two students offer models of what a chalk stick is made of.
Model A (Tanvi): 'Chalk is one continuous substance with no smaller units inside it. Grinding simply cuts it into smaller pieces of chalk, and you could go on cutting for ever.'
Model B (Imran): 'Chalk is made of a very large number of extremely small units held together by attraction.'
(a) The chapter says the grinding activity supports Model B. What does grinding show about each speck, and which claim of Model A does it not settle by itself? (1)
(b) Use the sugar activity to give the evidence that favours Model B, explaining what each observation shows. (2)
(c) Model B says the units are 'held together by attraction'. What everyday fact about a chalk stick does this part of the model explain, and what is this attraction called? (1)
(d) State which model the chapter supports and the one claim of Model A that the chapter directly contradicts. (1)
questions.a: (a) Grinding shows that each speck, however small, is still chalk and can be broken further, which fits a substance made of very many small units. By itself it does not show where the dividing stops, so it does not settle Model A's claim that cutting could go on for ever. (b) After stirring, no sugar can be seen, yet every spoonful, even from the top layer, tastes sweet. So the sugar is still present but has broken into pieces far too small to see that have spread through all the water and occupy the spaces between water particles. This is what Model B expects: a substance made of extremely small units can separate into them. (c) It explains why a chalk stick stays together as one solid piece instead of falling apart; the forces are called interparticle attractions. (d) The chapter supports Model B. It contradicts Model A's claim that division could go on for ever: the chapter says grinding would eventually reach a stage where the chalk particles cannot be broken down any further, the constituent particles.
s: (a) each speck is still chalk and can be broken further; grinding alone does not show where dividing stops
(b) invisible yet sweet everywhere: sugar broken into extremely small units spread through the water
(c) attraction explains why the stick holds together; named interparticle attraction
(d) Model B supported; Model A's endless division contradicted by the stage where particles cannot be broken further

Match each observation in Column I with what it shows in Column II.
Column I
1. No new substance forms when chalk is ground to powder
2. Sweet water in which no sugar can be seen

c. Particles can be sensed by taste though not seen
d. Grains are not the smallest units of rock

Reason (R): Chalk is a soft solid that can easily be broken and ground into a fine powder.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

questions.q:
A brick wall is built from hundreds of bricks, and each brick is made of baked clay.
(a) In the chapter's meaning of the term, is a brick a constituent particle of the wall? Say yes or no.
(b) Give the reason for your answer using the chapter's description of a constituent particle.
questions.a: (a) No. (b) The chapter describes a constituent particle as the basic unit of a substance, reached only when it cannot be broken down any further, and far too small to see. A brick can easily be broken into smaller pieces of clay, and each piece is made of a very large number of constituent particles, so a brick is not one.
s: (a) no
(b) a constituent particle cannot be broken further and is too small to see; a brick can be broken and is visible

questions.q: Ankit says that ice, liquid water and steam must be three different substances because they are in three different states. Which idea from the chapter best corrects him?
questions.a: How strongly the same particles attract decides the state
o: How strongly the same particles attract decides the state
Each state of matter is made of its own kind of particle
Only solids are made of particles; liquids and gases are not
The state is decided by the size of each constituent particle

questions.q: Show that a single grain of sugar cannot be just one constituent particle of sugar, using what happens when the grain is stirred into a glass of water.
questions.a: A grain of sugar is big enough to be seen, but constituent particles are too small to be seen even through an ordinary microscope. When the grain is stirred into water it disappears from view, yet the sweetness reaches every part of the glass, even the top layer. One particle could not spread to sweeten the whole glass; the grain must have broken up into a very large number of particles that spread through all the water. So each grain is made up of millions and millions of constituent particles, not one.
s: a visible grain is far bigger than an invisible constituent particle
on dissolving, the sweetness spreads through the whole glass though nothing is seen
so the grain broke into a very large number of particles; it is not a single particle

questions.q:
A student writes: 'Particles of every substance attract each other with exactly the same strength, so the state of a substance depends only on how far apart its particles are.'
(a) Name the factor his statement leaves out.
(b) State what the strength of these attractions finally decides about a substance, and give one example of the result the student cannot explain with his statement.
questions.a: (a) The strength of interparticle attraction also depends on the nature of the substance, not only on the interparticle distance. (b) The strength decides the physical state of the substance. Example: at room temperature iron is a solid while water is a liquid; the two are different substances whose particles attract with different strengths, which his 'same strength for all' idea cannot explain.
s: (a) nature of the substance left out
(b) strength decides the physical state, with a valid example of two different substances in different states

questions.q:
A science video uses a simple model for one substance. It gives the attraction between two of its particles, in made-up units, for different gaps between them.
Gap between particles | Attraction
1.0 | 100
1.1 | 60
1.5 | 5
2.0 | almost 0
(a) The chapter says that even a slight increase in the distance decreases the interparticle force drastically. Use the first two rows to test whether the model agrees.
(b) Predict a range for the attraction at a gap of 1.05, and explain.
(c) For a second substance, the video gives an attraction of only 30 at a gap of 1.0. Which factor named in the chapter explains why two substances differ at the same gap?
(d) A student's notes say: 'At a gap of 1.5 the attraction is stronger than at 1.1, because the particles have more room to pull on each other.' Find the error and correct it using the table.
questions.a: (a) It agrees: a 10% increase in the gap (1.0 to 1.1) makes the attraction fall from 100 to 60, a fall of 40%, which is a drastic fall for a slight increase in distance. (b) Between 60 and 100: 1.05 lies between 1.0 and 1.1, and the attraction falls as the gap grows, so it must be less than 100 and more than 60. (c) The nature of the substance: the chapter says the strength of interparticle attraction depends on the nature of the substance as well as on the distance. (d) The note is wrong: the table shows 5 at a gap of 1.5 against 60 at 1.1, so the attraction is much weaker at the larger gap; attraction falls as particles move farther apart, it does not grow.
s: (a) 10% more gap gives a 40% fall in attraction, so the model agrees
(b) between 60 and 100, because attraction falls as the gap grows
(c) the nature of the substance
(d) error found: attraction at 1.5 (5) is weaker than at 1.1 (60)

questions.q:
Kavya snaps a chalk stick into two pieces. The broken surfaces are rough, so when she presses them together they touch only at a few points and most of the particles on the two faces stay a little farther apart than they were inside the stick. The pieces never join back into one.
(a) What normally holds the constituent particles of the stick together as one piece?
(b) Using the premise above and what the chapter says about how this hold depends on distance, explain why the pieces do not rejoin.
questions.a: (a) Interparticle attractions, the attractive forces between the constituent particles. (b) The strength of these attractions falls drastically with even a slight increase in interparticle distance. Because the rough faces touch only at a few points, most of their particles stay a little farther apart than inside the stick, so the attraction across the break is far too weak to hold the pieces as one.
s: (a) interparticle attractions hold the particles together
(b) even a slight increase in distance drastically weakens the attraction; the ends cannot be brought that close again

questions.q:
On a trip, a geography teacher shows her class a rock from a Himalayan hillside, a rounded pebble from the Ganga at Haridwar and a pinch of fine sand from the riverbank at Patna, and tells them that the pebble and the sand both come from rock like this one.
(a) The pebble is rounded and much smaller than the rock. Explain what this tells you about what happened to it on its way down the river. (1)
(b) Rahul says, 'I cannot break a grain of sand with my fingers, so sand must be the smallest possible piece of rock.' Use the chalk activity to show why his reasoning fails. (2)
(c) The chapter says sand grains are made of their constituent particles. Explain why no one on the trip, even with a good magnifying glass, could see one of these particles. (1)
(d) Rock, pebble and sand differ greatly in size. State what stays the same in all three, according to the chapter, and why. (1)
questions.a: (a) It was broken down from a bigger piece: the river carried the eroded rock and kept breaking it down as it flowed, so the piece became smaller (and was worn round); the same process continues to give sand. (b) A chalk bit that is too small to break by hand can still be ground into a finer powder in a mortar, and each speck is still chalk; being unable to break something by hand does not mean it cannot be broken further. In the same way a sand grain can be broken further and is not the smallest unit of rock. (c) Constituent particles are so small that they cannot be seen even through an ordinary microscope, let alone a magnifying glass. (d) All three are made of the same kind of constituent particles, because they come from the same rock and breaking is only a change of size; only the number of particles in each piece differs.
s: (a) the pebble was broken down from bigger rock as the river carried it
(b) chalk too small to break by hand can still be ground finer and is still chalk, so sand is not the smallest unit
(c) constituent particles cannot be seen even through an ordinary microscope
(d) same constituent particles, since all come from the same rock; only their number differs

questions.q: Describe an everyday material (not chalk, sand, clay or sugar) that can be broken into smaller and smaller pieces that are still the same material. Explain what the pieces show, and what the chapter says about where this breaking must finally stop.
questions.a: Any valid example, such as a lump of jaggery or a piece of rock salt crushed in a mortar: each smaller piece is still jaggery (or rock salt), because breaking is a physical change that only reduces the size. This shows the material is made of a very large number of smaller units. The chapter says that if the breaking could go on, a stage would finally be reached where the pieces cannot be broken down any further: these are the constituent particles, far too small to be seen even through an ordinary microscope.
s: a valid material whose pieces stay the same material
breaking is a physical change, so pieces show the material is made of many smaller units
breaking stops at constituent particles that cannot be broken further and cannot be seen

questions.q: Two spoons of sugar are stirred into a glass of water until no sugar can be seen. Where have the sugar particles gone?
questions.a: Into the spaces between the particles of the water
o: Into the spaces between the particles of the water
They have turned into extra particles of water
Down to the bottom of the glass, as a thin layer
Out of the glass into the air, while being stirred

questions.q: Nisha fills a plastic bottle to the brim with water, closes it and leaves it in the freezer overnight. In the morning the water has frozen and the bottle bulges outwards. Which fact from the chapter fits this observation?
questions.a: Ice particles are farther apart than water particles
o: Ice particles are farther apart than water particles
Ice particles vibrate faster than water particles do
Freezing adds extra particles to the water in the bottle
Ice particles are closer together than water particles

questions.q:
Assertion (A): When urea is heated to 133 °C and melts, the attraction between its particles becomes stronger.
Reason (R): On melting, the particles of a solid start leaving their fixed positions.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true
o: A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false

questions.q:
A piece of aluminium and a stone are each moved from a flat tray into a narrow glass tumbler.
(a) State what happens to the shape and the volume of each object.
(b) Give the particle-level reason for (a), naming the force involved.
questions.a: (a) Neither changes: each keeps its own shape and its own volume in the tumbler. (b) In solids the particles are tightly packed and held in fixed positions by very strong interparticle attractions; they can only vibrate about those positions and cannot move past each other, so the object cannot spread out or take the tumbler's shape.
s: (a) both keep their shape and volume
(b) tightly packed particles held in fixed positions by strong interparticle attraction, unable to move past each other

questions.q:
A school lab in Lucknow heated four unlabelled solids slowly and noted the temperature at which each one started to melt.
Solid | Starts to melt at
P | 44 °C
Q | 80 °C
R | 121 °C
S | 327 °C
(a) Rank the four solids from the weakest to the strongest interparticle attraction, and give the rule you used.
(b) The solids are kept at 60 °C. State the physical state of P and of R, and describe how the particles of each are moving.
(c) Q was warmed from 30 °C to 70 °C and did not melt. What was happening to its particles during this warming, and why did they not leave their positions?
(d) The club wants to melt one solid, pour it into moulds and let it set into figures. Its only heater is a pan of boiling water (100 °C), and the figures will stand on a windowsill that reaches 50 °C in May. Decide which solid to use and rule out each of the others.
questions.a: (a) P, Q, R, S (weakest to strongest). Rule: weak interparticle attraction gives a low melting point, strong attraction a high one. (b) P (melting point 44 °C) is a liquid: its particles have left their fixed positions and move about, but only within a limited space. R (121 °C) is still a solid: its particles only vibrate about fixed positions. (c) Its particles vibrated more and more vigorously as it was heated, but below 80 °C the vibrations were not yet vigorous enough to overcome the attraction holding them, so they stayed in their positions. (d) Q. It melts at 80 °C, below the 100 °C the pan can reach, and stays solid on a 50 °C windowsill. P would melt on the windowsill (44 °C is below 50 °C); R (121 °C) and S (327 °C) cannot be melted in boiling water.
s: (a) P, Q, R, S with the rule weak attraction gives a low melting point
(b) P liquid, particles moving within a limited space; R solid, particles only vibrating
(c) vibrations increase but are not vigorous enough to leave fixed positions below 80 °C
(d) Q chosen; P melts on the sill, R and S cannot be melted at 100 °C

questions.q: Tanya compares an iron key with the water in a glass beside it. Which statement about the particles of the key, compared with those of the water, is correct?
questions.a: They are more tightly packed and held more strongly
o: They are more tightly packed and held more strongly
They are farther apart, so the key keeps its own shape
They move past one another more easily than water's
They are held more weakly, since the key does not flow

questions.q: Sneha tells her friend, 'In a solid the particles are packed so tightly that they do not move at all. They start moving only when the solid melts.' Check her claim and correct it.
questions.a: No, the claim is wrong. Particles in a solid are tightly packed and held in fixed positions, but they are not still: they move to and fro about their positions (vibrate or oscillate). What they cannot do is move past each other. When the solid is heated these vibrations become more vigorous; melting is the stage at which the vibrations become so vigorous that the particles start leaving their positions, not the point at which movement begins.
s: verdict: wrong
solid particles vibrate about fixed positions but cannot move past each other
heating makes vibrations more vigorous; at melting the particles leave their positions

questions.q:
Match each case in Column I with the description in Column II.
Column I
1. Ice, which melts at 0 °C
2. Iron, which needs the highest temperature of the three to melt
3. A stone that does not spread into the shape of a jar
4. Urea heated to 140 °C
Column II
a. Very strong interparticle attraction, high melting point
b. A liquid whose particles have left their fixed positions
c. Weak interparticle attraction, low melting point
d. Keeps its own shape because its particles cannot move past each other

These four statements describe a solid being heated up to its melting point.
(i) Its particles vibrate more vigorously.
(ii) Its particles start leaving their fixed positions.
(iii) The interparticle attractions get weakened.
(iv) Its particles break up into smaller constituent particles.
(a) Which statement is the odd one out?
(b) Explain why it does not belong.
questions.a: (a) Statement (iv). (b) Constituent particles are the basic units that cannot be broken down any further. Melting only changes how the same particles are held and how they move (they vibrate more, leave their positions as the attraction weakens); the particles themselves do not break up.
s: (a) statement (iv)
(b) constituent particles do not break up; melting changes only their movement and attraction

Consider these statements about solids and melting.
Statement 1: A solid whose interparticle forces are weak has a low melting point.
Statement 2: At its melting point, a solid's particles start moving freely in all directions.
Statement 3: For most substances the particles are a little farther apart in the liquid state than in the solid state, but ice is an exception.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
'The melting point is a property of the substance, not of the size of the piece.' Justify this statement in parts.
(a) Describe what happens to the particles of a solid at its melting point. (1)
(b) Explain why a large block of ice and a small ice cube both start to melt at 0 °C. (2)
(c) Use Table 7.1 (ice 0 °C, urea 133 °C, iron 1538 °C) to show that changing the substance does change the melting point, and give the reason. (1)
(d) Dev says a thin iron wire should melt at a much lower temperature than a thick iron rod. Use (b) to judge his idea. (1)
questions.a: (a) The particles, vibrating more and more vigorously as the solid is heated, start leaving their fixed positions; the attractions weaken and the solid turns into a liquid. (b) Both pieces are the same substance, so their particles are held by attractions of the same strength (the strength depends on the nature of the substance and the distance between particles, not on how big the piece is). The vibrations needed to free the particles are reached at the same temperature, 0 °C, in both. (c) Ice, urea and iron are different substances with different strengths of interparticle attraction: ice has weak forces and melts at 0 °C, urea melts at 133 °C, and iron has very strong forces and melts at 1538 °C. (d) His idea is wrong: the wire and the rod are both iron with the same interparticle attraction, so both start melting at 1538 °C; only the size differs.
s: (a) particles leave their fixed positions as attraction weakens
(b) same substance means the same attraction, so the same melting temperature whatever the size
(c) different substances have different attraction strengths, shown by 0, 133 and 1538 °C
(d) wire and rod are both iron, so both melt at 1538 °C

questions.q: Samples of the three solids in Table 7.1 (ice 0 °C, urea 133 °C, iron 1538 °C) are put on a hot plate kept at 140 °C and left there for a while. The number of these samples still in the solid state is ___.
True or false? 'The particles of a solid can be moving all the time and the solid can still keep a perfectly fixed shape.' Give your verdict and explain it.
questions.a: True. The particles of a solid are always vibrating (moving to and fro) about their fixed positions, but strong interparticle attractions stop them from moving past each other. Since no particle leaves its position, the shape stays fixed even though the particles are moving.
s: verdict: true
particles vibrate about fixed positions but cannot move past each other, so the shape stays fixed

questions.q:
Arjun heated a solid sample slowly in a water bath. The sample started to melt at 62 °C. He wrote what the particles were doing at each temperature, but two lines of his record are wrong.
Temperature | Arjun's note on the particles
30 °C | held in fixed positions, vibrating
55 °C | vibrating more vigorously and have left their fixed positions
62 °C | vibrations so vigorous that they start leaving their positions; the solid turns into a liquid
75 °C | back in fixed positions, only vibrating, though the sample is a liquid
(a) Find the error in the 55 °C line and correct it.
(b) Find the error in the 75 °C line and correct it.
(c) Arjun leaves another sample on a hot plate held at exactly 60 °C for an hour. Predict its state at the end and describe its particles.
(d) In the same bath, a classmate's sample of a different solid was still solid at 62 °C and started melting only at 90 °C. What can you conclude about its interparticle attraction compared with Arjun's sample, and why?
questions.a: (a) At 55 °C the sample is below its melting point, so the particles are vibrating more vigorously but have not yet left their fixed positions; the solid is still a solid. (b) At 75 °C the sample is a liquid, so its particles are not in fixed positions: they move about, though only within a limited space. (c) It will still be solid after the hour: 60 °C is below the minimum temperature at which it melts (62 °C), so its particles vibrate vigorously but stay in their fixed positions; waiting longer does not change that. (d) The classmate's solid has stronger interparticle attraction: its particles need more vigorous vibrations, reached only at the higher temperature of 90 °C, before they can leave their positions; strong attractive forces give a high melting point.
s: (a) at 55 °C particles vibrate more but stay in fixed positions
(b) at 75 °C liquid particles move within a limited space, not fixed
(c) still solid at 60 °C, below the melting point; particles only vibrate
(d) stronger attraction, since a higher melting point needs more vigorous vibrations

questions.q:
A steel ice-cube tray is filled exactly level with water and put in a freezer. Next morning the ice stands slightly above the rim.
(a) State the general rule in the chapter about particle spacing in the solid and liquid states.
(b) Explain how ice breaks this rule and how that accounts for the tray.
(c) Predict whether a 1-litre bottle of cooking oil, which follows the general rule, will take up more or less space after it turns solid in the cold. Give your reason.
questions.a: (a) Generally, particles in the liquid state are somewhat farther apart than in the solid state. (b) Ice is the exception: its particles are farther apart than those in liquid water, so the same water takes up more space as ice and rises above the rim. (c) Less space: for a substance that follows the general rule, the particles come a little closer together in the solid state than in the liquid, so the solid oil occupies a little less space than the liquid did.
s: (a) liquid particles are generally farther apart than solid particles
(b) ice particles are farther apart than water particles, so the ice takes more space
(c) predicts less space, because particles of the solid are closer than in the liquid

questions.q: A sample of a solid on a hot plate first starts to melt when the plate reaches 70 °C. Leela puts a second sample of the same solid straight onto a plate at 90 °C, and it melts too. What is the melting point of the solid?

A team in Chennai has an unknown solid Z. They put one sample of Z into each of four water baths, each kept at a fixed temperature for 10 minutes, and wrote what they saw.
Bath | Temperature | Z after 10 minutes
1 | 40 °C | still solid
2 | 55 °C | still solid
3 | 70 °C | melted
4 | 85 °C | melted
(a) Working back from the results, between which two temperatures does the melting point of Z lie? Use the meaning of melting point to explain.
(b) In Bath 2 the sample warmed by 30 degrees above the room temperature of 25 °C and yet did not melt. Describe what its particles were doing.
(c) Is the interparticle attraction in Z stronger or weaker than in urea (133 °C), and than in ice (0 °C)? Explain.
(d) The team may set up only two more baths and wants to pin the melting point down to a range of 5 degrees. Decide the two bath temperatures they should use and explain how the results would then show the range.
questions.a: (a) Above 55 °C and at most 70 °C. The melting point is the minimum temperature at which the solid melts: Z did not melt at 55 °C, so its melting point is higher than 55 °C; it did melt at 70 °C, so its melting point is not above 70 °C. (b) Its particles were vibrating more vigorously than at room temperature, but still only about their fixed positions; the vibrations were not vigorous enough for them to leave their positions. (c) Weaker than in urea, since Z melts below 70 °C while urea needs 133 °C; stronger than in ice, since Z is still solid at 55 °C while ice melts at 0 °C. (d) 60 °C and 65 °C. These split the 15-degree gap from 55 °C to 70 °C into three 5-degree parts: if Z melts at 60 °C the melting point is above 55 and at most 60; if it melts at 65 °C but not 60 °C it lies above 60 and at most 65; if it melts at neither, it lies above 65 and at most 70.
s: (a) above 55 °C and at most 70 °C, using minimum melting temperature
(b) particles vibrate more vigorously but stay in fixed positions
(c) weaker than urea, stronger than ice, with the reason from the temperatures
(d) baths at 60 °C and 65 °C, with how each outcome gives a 5-degree range

questions.q:
(a) Explain why the particles of a solid start leaving their fixed positions only after the solid has been heated a great deal, and not as soon as heating begins.
(b) Once the particles have left their fixed positions, state two ways in which the behaviour of the substance changes.
questions.a: (a) The particles are held in place by strong interparticle attractions. Heating makes them vibrate more vigorously, but only when the vibrations become vigorous enough to overcome these attractions (at the melting point) can the particles leave their positions. (b) Any two: it no longer has a definite shape and takes the shape of its container; its particles can now move past each other, so it can flow; it is now a liquid with particles moving within a limited space.
s: (a) vibrations must become vigorous enough to overcome strong attraction
(b) two changes, e.g. no fixed shape and able to flow

questions.q:
A revision card on solids has three lines.
Line 1: 'A solid has a definite shape, but its volume changes to fit the container it is put in.'
Line 2: 'The particles of a solid vibrate about fixed positions.'
Line 3: 'A solid melts when its particles stop vibrating.'
Find the two wrong lines, correct them, and give the particle reason for each correction.
questions.a: Line 1 is wrong: a solid has a definite shape and a definite volume; its particles are tightly packed and held in fixed positions by strong attraction, so neither its shape nor its volume changes with the container. Line 3 is wrong: on heating the particles vibrate more and more vigorously, and the solid melts when the vibrations become so vigorous that the particles start leaving their fixed positions. Line 2 is right.
s: Line 1 corrected: definite volume too, because particles are tightly packed in fixed positions
Line 3 corrected: melting happens when vibrations become vigorous enough to leave positions
Line 2 identified as right

questions.q:
Of the objects in Activity 7.3 (iron nail, rock salt, stone, wood, key, aluminium), a student says, 'Wood cannot really be a solid, because a carpenter can cut and carve it into any shape he likes.'
(a) Does cutting wood show that it lacks a definite shape? Say yes or no and why.
(b) Explain, using particles, what a definite shape means for each piece of wood.
questions.a: (a) No. Cutting applies a force that breaks the wood; each cut piece still keeps its own shape and volume and does not change shape by itself or take the shape of a container. (b) In each piece the particles are tightly packed and held in fixed positions by strong attraction; they can only vibrate and cannot move past each other, so the piece holds its shape.
s: (a) no: a cut piece still keeps its own shape and volume
(b) particles held in fixed positions, cannot move past each other

questions.q:
A sample of urea and an iron nail are placed side by side on a hot plate and warmed slowly from 25 °C to 140 °C. Compare and analyse what happens.
(a) Describe the state of each and the movement of its particles at 100 °C. (1)
(b) Describe the state of each and the movement of its particles at 140 °C. (2)
(c) Explain the difference at 140 °C in terms of interparticle attraction. (1)
(d) State what would have to be done for the iron to change in the way the urea did, and why. (1)
questions.a: (a) Both are still solid; the particles of each vibrate more vigorously than at 25 °C but stay in their fixed positions. (b) Urea has melted (it melts at 133 °C): its particles have left their fixed positions and move about, though only within a limited space. Iron is still solid: its particles vibrate more vigorously than before but remain in fixed positions. (c) The interparticle attraction in urea is much weaker than in iron, so urea's particles can leave their positions at 133 °C while iron's strong attraction holds its particles until 1538 °C. (d) The iron would have to be heated to its melting point of 1538 °C, because only then do its vibrations become vigorous enough to overcome its very strong interparticle attraction.
s: (a) both solid at 100 °C, particles vibrating more vigorously in fixed positions
(b) urea liquid with particles moving in a limited space; iron solid with particles vibrating
(c) urea's attraction much weaker than iron's
(d) heat iron to 1538 °C to overcome its strong attraction

questions.q:
A group in Bhopal marked the 250 mL level on three containers of very different shapes: a tall jar J, a wide bowl K and a conical flask L. J and L had been washed and dried; K had been left unwashed after an earlier experiment. They filled J to the mark and poured the same water, without spilling, from J into K and then from K into L.
Container | Reading
J (clean) | 250 mL
K (unwashed) | 250 mL
L (clean) | 247 mL
(a) The water looked completely different in each container. Explain, using particles, why the same water could take three different shapes.
(b) Which container caused the drop in the reading, and how can you tell from the order of the readings?
(c) A group member concludes, 'The 247 mL reading proves that liquids do not have a definite volume.' Correct this conclusion.
(d) There is time for one more demonstration to convince the class, ending with a reading in a fresh container. Plan X: pour the water from L into a fourth clean, dry container M and read M. Plan Y: pour it from L back into the still-unwashed K, then from K into a clean, dry container N and read N. Decide which plan to use and justify your choice by predicting the final reading of each.
questions.a: (a) The particles of a liquid are free to move (they can move past each other), so the water flows and takes the shape of whichever container it is in. (b) K. The reading in K was still 250 mL, but the drop appeared in the next container, L: some water stuck to the walls of the unwashed K and was left behind when it was poured out. (c) Liquids do have a definite volume; the water was not reduced in volume, a little of it was simply left sticking to the walls of K. In clean containers the level stays the same in every container. (d) Plan X. Pouring from clean L into clean, dry M should leave the reading at 247 mL, showing that the volume stays fixed while the shape changes. In Plan Y the water is poured out of the unwashed K a second time, so some more water would stick to K's walls and N would read less than 247 mL; the drop would wrongly look like a change in volume and confuse the class.
s: (a) liquid particles are free to move, so the water takes the container's shape
(b) K, because the drop shows up in the container poured into after K
(c) the volume is definite; the missing water stuck to K's walls
(d) Plan X: M reads 247 mL; in Plan Y water sticks to K again, so N reads less

questions.q:
A student's chart describes three unnamed samples.
S: particles closely packed, only vibrate
T: particles a little loosely packed, move within a limited space
U: particles free, move through all the available space
Which sample would keep the same volume in containers of any shape while taking each container's shape?
questions.a: Sample T, as its particles move only in a limited space
o: Sample T, as its particles move only in a limited space
Sample S, as its particles are the most closely packed
Sample U, as its particles move through all the space
Both T and U, since the particles of both are able to move

questions.q: True or false? 'Water in an open bowl turns into vapour only after it is heated to its boiling point.' Give your verdict and the correct idea.
questions.a: False. Vapour forms from a liquid at all temperatures, even below the boiling point, but slowly and only at the surface: this is evaporation, which is why spilled water dries up at room temperature. At the boiling point the formation of vapour becomes very fast and also occurs within the liquid.
s: verdict: false
vapour forms at all temperatures, slowly at the surface (evaporation); boiling is only the fast stage

questions.q: Raghav easily moves his hand through a bucket of water, and the water closes up again when he takes it out. He cannot push his finger into a block of ice at all without breaking it. Which comparison do these observations support?
questions.a: Attraction in water is slightly weaker than in ice
o: Attraction in water is slightly weaker than in ice
Water particles have no attraction between them at all
Water particles are fixed, while ice particles move about
Attraction in water is much stronger than it is in ice

questions.q: Pallavi pulls her finger out of a bowl of water and watches the gap close at once. She says, 'This shows that water particles can move, but they still attract each other strongly enough to stay close together.' Is she right? Explain what each half of her observation shows.
questions.a: Yes, she is right. Being able to move a finger through the water without cutting it permanently, which cannot be done with a solid, shows that the particles can move and that the attraction in a liquid is slightly weaker than in a solid. The water returning to its position as soon as the finger is removed shows that the attraction is still strong enough to keep the particles close together.
s: verdict: right
finger passes through without permanent cut: particles move, attraction slightly weaker than in solids
water closes up again: attraction still strong enough to keep particles close

questions.q:
Consider these statements about liquids.
Statement 1: The particles of a liquid are free to move, but only within a limited space.
Statement 2: At the boiling point, vapour forms inside the liquid as well as at its surface.
Statement 3: In a liquid, the interparticle attraction is slightly weaker than in a solid.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1, 2 and 3
o: 1, 2 and 3
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 only

questions.q:
Rani's mother pours 1 litre of oil from a tall bottle into a wide frying pan, where it spreads into a thin layer. Rani says, 'The oil has become less now.'
(a) Is Rani right? Say what has changed and what has not.
(b) Explain, using particles, why the oil spreads out yet keeps its volume.
questions.a: (a) No. Only the shape has changed; the volume is still 1 litre (liquids have a definite volume). (b) The particles of a liquid are free to move, so the oil flows and takes the shape of the pan; but they move only within a limited space, held close together by interparticle attraction, so the volume does not change.
s: (a) not right: shape changed, volume still 1 litre
(b) particles free to move (shape) but held close within a limited space (volume)

questions.q: Neha pours 200 mL of water from a clean jug into a bottle whose inside walls are still wet with oil from an earlier use, and then from the bottle into a clean, dry glass. What should the glass read?
questions.a: A little less than 200 mL
o: A little less than 200 mL
Exactly 200 mL, as liquids keep their volume
A little more than 200 mL
About 100 mL, as the oily bottle takes half

questions.q: A clear liquid is heated slowly in an open beaker at atmospheric pressure. At 50 °C and at 64 °C it is not bubbling; at 78 °C bubbles start forming all through the liquid, and the thermometer stays at 78 °C while it keeps bubbling. The boiling point of this liquid is ___ °C.
Honey poured from a jar spreads out to take the shape of a bowl, but a pebble dropped into the same bowl keeps its own shape. What explains the difference?
questions.a: Honey's particles can move past one another; the pebble's cannot
o: Honey's particles can move past one another; the pebble's cannot
Honey has no attraction at all between its particles, unlike the pebble
Honey's particles are much farther apart than those of a gas
The pebble's particles stop moving once it touches the bowl

questions.q:
Two identical steel dishes each hold 100 mL of water. Dish A stands on a windowsill at 30 °C and loses 6 mL in 4 hours. Dish B is boiled on a stove at 100 °C and loses 60 mL in 10 minutes.
(a) Work out how many millilitres each dish loses in one hour, and how many times faster Dish B loses water. (1)
(b) Name the process in each dish. (1)
(c) Explain why the loss in Dish B is so much faster, saying where vapour forms in each dish. (2)
(d) Nothing was spilled from Dish B, yet 60 mL of water is gone. Where have those water particles gone, and in what state are they now? (1)
questions.a: (a) Dish A: 6 / 4 = 1.5 mL per hour. Dish B: 60 / 10 = 6 mL per minute = 360 mL per hour. Dish B loses water 360 / 1.5 = 240 times faster. (b) Dish A: evaporation. Dish B: boiling. (c) At 30 °C, below the boiling point, vapour forms only at the surface and slowly. At the boiling point the movement of particles becomes so vigorous that they move apart and escape, and vapour forms very fast, not only at the surface but also within the liquid. (d) The particles escaped from the liquid and are now in the air as vapour, that is, in the gaseous state; the water has not been destroyed.
s: (a) 1.5 mL per hour, 360 mL per hour, 240 times
(b) evaporation in A, boiling in B
(c) A: slow, surface only; B: fast, at the surface and within the liquid as particles escape
(d) particles escaped into the air as vapour (gaseous state), not destroyed

questions.q:
A wall chart lists, for the liquid state: 'Particles are closely packed. Interparticle attraction is maximum.'
(a) Correct both entries for a liquid.
(b) Name the state that the two original entries actually describe, and give one observation from the chapter showing that a liquid's attraction is weaker than that state's.
questions.a: (a) In a liquid the particles are a little more loosely packed than in a solid, and the interparticle attraction is slightly weaker than in a solid (though still strong enough to keep the particles close). (b) The solid state. Observation: a finger can be moved through water without cutting it permanently, which cannot be done with a solid.
s: (a) a little loosely packed; attraction slightly weaker than in solids
(b) solid state, with the finger-through-water observation

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Water takes the shape of whatever container it is poured into.
Reason (R): The interparticle attraction in water is strong enough to keep its particles close together.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
Sameer drew a three-panel strip to show water boiling in a pan and wrote a caption under each panel.
Panel 1 (water at room temperature): 'The particles vibrate in fixed positions, like those of a solid.'
Panel 2 (water close to its boiling point): 'The particles move more vigorously and move apart, so the attraction between them decreases.'
Panel 3 (water at its boiling point): 'The particles escape because the attraction between them becomes stronger as they move apart.'
Find the two wrong captions and correct them. Say which caption is right.
questions.a: Panel 1 is wrong: in a liquid the particles are not held in fixed positions; they are free to move, though only within a limited space. Panel 3 is wrong: as the particles move apart the interparticle attraction decreases (even a slight increase in distance weakens it drastically), and it is this weakening that lets the particles escape from the liquid as vapour. Panel 2 is right: near the boiling point the particles move so vigorously that they move apart and the attraction decreases.
s: Panel 1 corrected: liquid particles move within a limited space, not fixed
Panel 3 corrected: moving apart weakens the attraction, which lets particles escape
Panel 2 identified as right, with the reason

questions.q:
Two cooks in a Hyderabad canteen each boil 1000 mL of water with dal in identical open pans. Both pans are bubbling all through the water. Cook A keeps the flame on high; Cook B turns it down until the water is only gently bubbling. A thermometer reads 100 °C in both pans. In the first 10 minutes, Pan A loses 300 mL of water and Pan B loses 120 mL.
(a) Explain how the bubbling all through the water shows that both pans are boiling, not just evaporating.
(b) Both pans read 100 °C although A has a much bigger flame. Using the meaning of boiling point and the water losses, explain where A's extra heat is going.
(c) The dal burns if the water falls below 400 mL. Working back from the rate of loss, find how many minutes Pan A can keep boiling from 1000 mL before it reaches 400 mL.
(d) The dal must boil for 30 minutes in all, counted from the start of boiling. Decide which flame setting the canteen should use and justify it with numbers.
questions.a: (a) In boiling, vapour forms within the liquid as well as at the surface, which is seen as bubbles throughout the water; evaporation happens only at the surface. (b) The boiling point is the temperature at which the liquid boils and turns into vapour (here 100 °C at atmospheric pressure), so both pans boil at the same temperature. The extra heat in A does not make the water hotter; it makes vapour form faster, which is why A loses 300 mL in 10 minutes against B's 120 mL. (c) A loses 300 / 10 = 30 mL per minute; (1000 - 400) / 30 = 20 minutes. (d) The low flame (B). In 30 minutes Pan A would lose 30 x 30 = 900 mL, leaving 100 mL, below 400 mL, so the dal would burn; Pan B loses 12 mL per minute, 12 x 30 = 360 mL, leaving 640 mL, while still boiling at the same 100 °C.
s: (a) bubbles throughout show vapour forming within the liquid, which happens only at boiling
(b) same boiling point in both; extra heat makes vapour form faster, shown by the larger loss
(c) 30 mL per minute, so 20 minutes
(d) low flame: A falls to 100 mL, B keeps 640 mL at the same temperature

questions.q: 200 mL of water and 200 mL of smoky air are each let into an empty closed 1-litre jar. Which observation shows that the particles of the liquid attract each other more strongly than those of the gas?
questions.a: The water stays at 200 mL; the smoke fills the jar
o: The water stays at 200 mL; the smoke fills the jar
Both take the shape of the 1-litre jar they are in
The smoke can be seen moving, but the water cannot
Both can be poured out when the jar is tipped over

questions.q: True or false? 'An ice cube and the water it melts into are made of the same particles; the difference is that the particles of the water can move past each other while those of the ice cannot.' Give your verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. Melting does not change the substance: the same particles are present, only how they are held changes. In ice the particles are held in fixed positions and can only vibrate; after melting they have left their fixed positions and can move past each other within a limited space, which is why water flows and takes the shape of its container.
s: verdict: true
same particles; in ice they only vibrate in fixed positions, in water they move past each other

questions.q:
Plan two simple tests, using only 200 mL of water, a wooden block, two containers of different shapes and your finger, that together show two differences between a liquid and a solid.
(a) Describe Test 1 and what you expect to see for the water and for the block. (2)
(b) Describe Test 2 and what you expect to see for the water and for the block. (1)
(c) For each of the two differences your tests show, give the particle-level reason. (2)
questions.a: Test 1: Pour the water from one container into the other, and move the wooden block from one container to the other. Expected: the water takes the shape of each container while its level stays at 200 mL; the block keeps its own shape in both. Test 2: Move a finger through the water, then try to push it into the block. Expected: the finger passes through the water, which closes up again; the finger cannot pass into the block without breaking it. Differences and reasons: (1) The liquid has no fixed shape but the solid does: liquid particles are free to move past each other within a limited space, while solid particles are held in fixed positions and only vibrate. (2) A finger can pass through the liquid but not the solid: interparticle attraction in a liquid is slightly weaker than in a solid, though still strong enough to keep the particles close, so the water closes up again.
s: (a) Test 1 described with expected results for both (shape changes for water, volume fixed; block unchanged)
(b) Test 2 described with expected results (finger passes through water, not the block)
(c) particle reasons for the two differences: free movement vs fixed positions; weaker attraction in liquids

questions.q: Show, using two different observations from the chapter, that the particles of water cannot be held in fixed positions the way the particles of a solid are.
questions.a: Observation 1: water poured into containers of different shapes takes the shape of each container. If its particles were held in fixed positions, like a solid's, the water would keep one shape. Observation 2: a finger can be moved through water, which closes up again as soon as the finger is removed; a finger cannot be moved through a solid without breaking it. Both show that the particles of water can move past each other, so they are not fixed in place; they move freely, though within a limited space.
s: observation 1: water takes each container's shape, which fixed particles could not do
observation 2: a finger passes through water and it closes up, unlike a solid
conclusion: water particles move past each other, so they are not fixed

questions.q:
Two liquids, P (boiling point 56 °C) and Q (boiling point 78 °C), are put in separate open beakers in a water bath kept at 70 °C.
(a) Which liquid will boil, and what will you see in it?
(b) Will the other liquid lose any vapour at all? Explain.
questions.a: (a) P will boil, because 70 °C is above its boiling point of 56 °C: bubbles of vapour will form within the liquid as well as at its surface. (b) Yes. Q will not boil, since 70 °C is below its boiling point of 78 °C, but vapour forms at all temperatures below the boiling point, slowly and only at the surface (evaporation), so Q will slowly lose some vapour.
s: (a) P boils, shown by bubbles forming within the liquid
(b) Q does not boil but evaporates slowly from its surface

questions.q: Three sealed 2-litre boxes each hold one substance. In box X it lies as a heap in one corner; in box Y it forms a layer with a flat surface at the bottom; in box Z nothing can be seen except a faint colour spread evenly from the floor to the lid. Which box holds a gas?
questions.a: Box Z, as its contents spread through the whole box
o: Box Z, as its contents spread through the whole box
Box Y, as its contents flow and take the box's shape
Box X, as its contents keep a shape of their own
Boxes Y and Z, as both of them flow and are fluids

questions.q:
The chapter says gases have no fixed shape, yet smoky air trapped in a cube-shaped glass box looks cube-shaped.
(a) Explain why there is no contradiction.
(b) Predict the shape of the smoky air if it is let from the box into an empty round flask, and give the particle reason.
questions.a: (a) Having no fixed shape means the gas has no shape of its own; it takes the shape of the vessel it is in, so in a cube-shaped box it is cube-shaped. (b) It will take the round shape of the flask (filling it), because gas particles move freely in all directions with negligible attraction, so nothing holds them in the cube's shape.
s: (a) no shape of its own; a gas takes the shape of its vessel
(b) round, the flask's shape, because particles move freely with negligible attraction

questions.q:
Smoky air is trapped in Gas Jar A. In three separate trials an empty jar B of the same size is joined to A with no gap: in Trial 1 B is placed above A, in Trial 2 below A, and in Trial 3 the two jars lie side by side on a table.
(a) Predict what will be seen in jar B after some time in Trial 1. (1)
(b) Predict the result in Trial 2 and in Trial 3. (2)
(c) Give the particle-level reason that makes your predictions in (b) the same as in (a). (1)
(d) A student expects smoke to move only upwards. Which trial would test her idea most directly, and what result would show she is wrong? (1)
questions.a: (a) The smoke spreads into jar B and fills it, until both jars look alike. (b) Trial 2 and Trial 3: the smoke also spreads into jar B and fills it, whether B is below A or beside it. (c) The particles of a gas move freely in all directions and the attraction between them is negligible, so the spreading does not depend on whether B is above, below or beside A; the smoke specks are carried along as the moving gas particles hit them. (d) Trial 2, with B below A: if the smoke spreads down into B and fills it, it is not moving only upwards.
s: (a) smoke spreads into B and fills it
(b) the same in Trials 2 and 3
(c) gas particles move freely in all directions with negligible attraction
(d) Trial 2; smoke filling the lower jar shows her idea is wrong

questions.q: Rank the attraction between particles from the strongest to the weakest in: a steel spoon, cooking oil in a bottle, and the water vapour above a pan.
questions.a: Steel spoon, cooking oil, water vapour
o: Steel spoon, cooking oil, water vapour
Cooking oil, steel spoon, water vapour
Water vapour, cooking oil, steel spoon
Steel spoon, water vapour, cooking oil

questions.q:
Consider these statements about gases.
Statement 1: A gas takes the shape of its container and has no fixed volume.
Statement 2: The interparticle attraction in a gas is stronger than in a liquid.
Statement 3: Iodine vapour formed in a closed jar stays near the crystals at the bottom of the jar.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 only
o: 1 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q:
In a Guwahati classroom, smoky air was trapped in Gas Jar A (1.5 litres). An identical empty jar B (1.5 litres) was then joined mouth to mouth with A so that no smoke could escape. The class noted what they saw.
Time | Jar A | Jar B
0 min | thick smoke | clear
1 min | smoke thinning | faint smoke near the joint
3 min | thin smoke | smoke spreading upwards
6 min | thin smoke | thin smoke, same as A
(a) Find the volume occupied by the smoky air at 0 minutes and at 6 minutes, and say what this shows about the volume of a gas.
(b) Explain, in terms of particles, why the smoky air did not stay in Jar A where it started.
(c) A classmate says the activity shows that a gas has no fixed shape as well. Point to what in the activity supports this.
(d) The class repeats the activity with a taller empty jar B that holds 3 litres. Predict what they will see at the end, the total volume the smoky air will occupy, and how thick the smoke will look compared with the first trial.
questions.a: (a) 1.5 litres at 0 minutes (Jar A only) and 1.5 + 1.5 = 3 litres at 6 minutes (both jars). The same gas came to occupy twice the space, so a gas has no fixed volume; it occupies the entire space available. (b) The particles of a gas move freely in all directions and the interparticle attraction between them is negligible, so nothing holds them in Jar A; they spread into Jar B. (c) At the end the smoky air had the shape of the two joined jars together, not the shape it had in Jar A alone, so it takes the shape of the vessel it is in. (d) The smoke will spread until it fills both jars evenly, occupying 1.5 + 3 = 4.5 litres; since the same smoke is spread through more space, it will look thinner than at the end of the first trial (when it filled 3 litres).
s: (a) 1.5 to 3 litres, so no fixed volume
(b) particles move freely in all directions with negligible attraction
(c) the gas took the shape of the two joined jars
(d) fills both jars, 4.5 litres, and looks thinner

questions.q:
A worksheet states: 'The spacing between particles is maximum in liquids, because liquids flow.'
(a) Which state actually has the maximum interparticle spacing, and how does the spacing in liquids compare with that in solids?
(b) Explain why a liquid can flow without having the maximum spacing.
questions.a: (a) Gases have the maximum interparticle spacing; in liquids the spacing is only a little more than in solids. (b) A liquid flows because its particles are free to move past each other (within a limited space), the attraction being slightly weaker than in solids; flowing needs this freedom of movement, not large spaces between the particles.
s: (a) gases have maximum spacing; liquids only a little more than solids
(b) flowing comes from particles moving past each other, not from large spacing

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Smoky air let into an empty gas jar spreads until it fills the entire jar.
Reason (R): The particles of a gas move freely in all directions, and the attraction between them is negligible.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

2 | common salt | 150 mL | 158 mL | 155 mL
3 | unknown white powder | 150 mL | 160 mL | 160 mL
(a) Group 3 says its powder is sand. Is the table consistent with this? Explain using where the particles go.
(b) For Group 1, compare the final volume with the sum of the volumes of the water and the sugar, and say what this shows about water.
(c) Explain, in terms of particles, why the level fell from B to C for Groups 1 and 2.
(d) Group 1 claims, 'Sugar made more volume disappear into the water's spaces than salt did, because our level fell more.' Test this claim fairly, taking into account how much of each solid was added.
questions.a: (a) Yes. Sand does not dissolve in water; its particles settle down and occupy their own space, so the level rises when it is added (150 to 160 mL) and does not fall on stirring (C = B = 160 mL), unlike a soluble solid. (b) The water (150 mL) and sugar (162 - 150 = 12 mL) add up to 162 mL, but the solution is only 158 mL, 4 mL less. The volume of the solution is less than the sum, which shows there is some space between the water particles. (c) On stirring, sugar and salt dissolved and broke up into their constituent particles, which occupied the spaces between the water particles, so the total volume became less than at B. (c) dissolved particles occupy the spaces between water particles
(d) claim tested per amount added: sugar 4/12 = 33%, salt 3/8 = 37.5%, so not supported

(c) By what percentage did the volume of the compressed syringe's contents decrease?

questions.a: (a) Air is compressible while water is practically incompressible. Syringe Q's contents shrank a lot (20 to 11 mL), which only air would do; P barely changed (20 to 19.8 mL), as water would. So P holds water and Q holds air. (b) While pushed, the gas particles in Q were forced closer together; when she let go, they spread out again and pushed the plunger back to its original position. (c) (20 - 11) / 20 x 100 = 45%. s: (a) large shrinkage means air (compressible); almost none means water, so labels are swapped

questions.a: (a) The sand particles settle down and occupy their own space in the container, so the total volume increases and stays up after stirring. (b) Water particles are in constant motion and pull particles out of a soluble solid such as sugar, spreading them through the water. In sand the constituent particles are held together so strongly that the water particles are unable to pull them out, so sand is insoluble. (c) The level will rise when the stones are added and will not fall on stirring, because stone, like sand, does not dissolve; its pieces occupy their own space instead of the spaces between water particles.

questions.q:

(b) Water is practically incompressible, yet there is evidence that it has some space between its particles. Give that evidence and explain how both facts fit together. (2)
(c) State what the chapter says about the spacing in solids and what that space contains. (1)
(d) Write the order of interparticle spacing and match it with the order of how easily each state can be compressed. (1)
questions.a: (a) Air shut in a syringe can be pushed into a smaller volume, and it springs back when released: there is a lot of space between gas particles that pressure can reduce. (b) When sugar dissolves in water, the solution's volume is less than the sum of the volumes of water and sugar, so there must be spaces between water particles that the sugar particles occupy. Both fit because these spaces are small, only a little more than in solids, enough to hold dissolved particles but leaving too little room for the water to be squeezed noticeably. (c) Even in solids, despite close packing, some space is left between particles, and it contains nothing at all, not air; it is the smallest of the three. (d) Spacing: solid < liquid < gas. Ease of compression follows the same order: solids and liquids practically cannot be compressed, gases can be compressed easily.

(b) dissolving sugar reduces total volume, so spaces exist; they are small, so water is practically incompressible
(c) solids have some space, which contains nothing at all
(d) solid < liquid < gas, matched with ease of compression

Tumbler | Water temperature | Time to turn uniformly pink

(a) Explain the trend in the times in terms of the movement of water particles.
(b) Predict, with a reason, a range for the time at 55 °C.
(c) Tumbler W took 15 minutes but did turn completely pink. What does this tell you about the water particles even at 6 °C?
(d) The teacher will repeat the demonstration in a 5-minute slot, and the school does not allow water above 50 °C in the classroom. Using the trend, decide the range of water temperatures she can rely on, and say why the data do not let her rely on any lower temperature.
questions.a: (a) Water particles move faster when they have more heat energy, so in warmer water they pull the potassium permanganate particles out and spread them faster; the movement of particles increases as heat is provided. (b) Between 2 and 4 minutes: 55 °C lies between 42 °C and 70 °C, so its particles should move faster than at 42 °C but slower than at 70 °C. (c) Even ice-cold water particles are in constant motion; they move more slowly, so the spreading is slower, but it still happens. (d) From 42 °C up to 50 °C. At 42 °C the colour spreads in 4 minutes, within the slot, and since the time falls as the temperature rises, any temperature between 42 °C and the 50 °C limit should take 4 minutes or less. The data give no time between 27 °C (7 minutes, too slow) and 42 °C, so she cannot be sure a lower temperature would finish within 5 minutes.
s: (a) more heat energy, faster particles, faster spreading
(b) between 2 and 4 minutes, with the reason
(c) particles are in constant motion even at 6 °C, only slower
(d) 42 °C to 50 °C, since time falls with temperature; no data between 27 °C and 42 °C

questions.q: After watching potassium permanganate spread in hot, room-temperature and ice-cold water, Sana says, 'The colour spreads fastest in hot water because hot water particles move faster and so spread the potassium permanganate faster. This shows that heating makes particles move more.' Do you agree? Explain.
questions.a: Yes, she is right. Water particles move faster in hot water than at room temperature, and slowest in ice-cold water. Faster-moving particles pull the potassium permanganate particles out of the grain and spread them more quickly, so the colour spreads fastest in hot water and slowest in ice-cold water. Since the only difference between the tumblers is how hot the water is, this shows that the movement of particles increases when heat is provided.
s: verdict: agree
particle movement is fastest in hot water and slowest in ice-cold water, so spreading follows the same order
only the temperature differed, so movement increases when heat is provided

questions.q:
Match each stage in Column I with the description of its particles in Column II.
Column I
1. A solid well below its melting point
2. A solid at its melting point
3. A liquid
4. A gas
Column II
a. Enough thermal energy to overcome the attraction; particles move freely in all directions
b. Low thermal energy; particles stay close and only vibrate
c. Particles move about, but only within a limited space
d. Thermal energy overcomes the attraction just enough for particles to leave their fixed positions

A lab notebook describes a sample K, without naming its state, at three temperatures.
20 °C: 'Particles very close together, held strongly, only vibrating.'
90 °C: 'Particles a little farther apart, moving about but only within a limited space.'
250 °C: 'Particles far apart, moving freely in all directions.'
(a) Name the state of K at each temperature. (1)
(b) Somewhere between 20 °C and 90 °C, K changed state. Name this temperature and explain what the thermal energy did to the particles there. (2)
(c) Explain why the particles at 250 °C can move freely when those at 90 °C cannot. (1)
(d) A classmate says K is three different substances, because the notebook describes three different kinds of particle behaviour. Judge this claim. (1)
questions.a: (a) 20 °C: solid; 90 °C: liquid; 250 °C: gas. (b) Its melting point. There, the thermal energy is used to overcome the attractive forces between the particles: the interparticle distance increases slightly, weakening the attraction to a level at which the particles can move away from their fixed positions and move around within a limited space. (c) At 250 °C the particles have enough thermal energy to overcome the forces of attraction between them almost completely, so they move freely in all directions; at 90 °C the attraction is still strong enough to keep them close, within a limited space. (d) The claim is wrong: the behaviour differs because the thermal energy of the same particles differs, and the chapter says it is the thermal energy of the particles that decides the physical state; it is one substance in three states.
s: (a) solid, liquid, gas
(b) melting point: thermal energy overcomes attraction, distance increases slightly, particles leave fixed positions
(c) enough energy at 250 °C to overcome attraction; at 90 °C attraction still keeps particles close
(d) wrong: same substance, different thermal energy decides the state

questions.q:
A grain of potassium permanganate and a grain of sand are dropped into two tumblers of water and left for an hour. The first tumbler turns pink; the sand grain lies unchanged at the bottom of the second.
(a) The water particles are moving in both tumblers. Explain why they spread the potassium permanganate but not the sand.
(b) What name does the chapter give to a substance that behaves like the sand?
questions.a: (a) In potassium permanganate the moving water particles can pull the particles out of the grain and then spread them. In sand, the constituent particles are held together so strongly that the water particles are unable to pull them out, so nothing spreads. (b) It is insoluble in water.
s: (a) sand's particles are held too strongly for the water particles to pull out
(b) insoluble
