questions.q:
The owner of a long, narrow sweet shop in Varanasi lights one incense stick every morning. With the fan off, his son noted when the fragrance was first smelled at different distances from the stick.
Distance from stick | Fragrance first smelled after
1 m | 1 min
3 m | 4 min
6 m | 9 min
(a) Explain why the fragrance is smelled near the stick first.
(b) Explain, in terms of particles, how the fragrance reaches 6 m although the air is still and the fan is off.
(c) His son says, 'The fragrance travels at the same speed all the way.' Use the table to test this.
(d) On a much colder winter morning, with the fan still off, will the fragrance reach the customer 6 m away sooner or later than 9 minutes? Predict, and justify with the chapter's idea about heat and particle movement.
questions.a: (a) The fragrance particles start at the stick, so they are most crowded there; they have not yet been spread far by the air particles. (b) The particles of air are constantly moving; they keep hitting the fragrance particles and help them spread through the whole room, so no wind or fan is needed. (c) It does not hold: the first 1 m took 1 minute, the next 2 m (1 to 3 m) took 3 minutes, and the next 3 m (3 to 6 m) took 5 minutes, so each metre takes longer the farther the fragrance has spread. (d) Later than 9 minutes. The chapter shows that the movement of particles increases when heat is provided, so in colder air the air particles move more slowly, hit the fragrance particles less vigorously and spread them more slowly.
s: (a) fragrance particles start at the stick and have not yet spread
(b) constantly moving air particles hit the fragrance particles and spread them
(c) not the same speed: 1 m in 1 min, 2 m in 3 min, 3 m in 5 min
(d) later, because colder air particles move more slowly and spread the fragrance more slowly

questions.q: Rohan says, 'At its melting point, a solid's particles get enough energy to move freely in all directions, just like the particles of a gas.' Check his claim.
questions.a: No, the claim is wrong. At the melting point the thermal energy only overcomes the attractive forces enough for the particles to move away from their fixed positions; the interparticle distance increases slightly, and the particles move around but still within a limited space, as in a liquid. Only in the gaseous state do the particles have enough energy to overcome the forces of attraction and move freely in all directions.
s: verdict: wrong
at the melting point particles leave fixed positions, distance increases slightly, movement within a limited space
free movement in all directions happens only in a gas, with enough energy to overcome the attraction

questions.q:
A solid L has its melting point at 50 °C.
(a) Compare the distance between L's particles and the way they move just below 50 °C and just after it has melted.
(b) Explain, using thermal energy, why this small change in distance is enough to let the particles move around.
questions.a: (a) Just below 50 °C the particles are close together in fixed positions and only vibrate; after melting the interparticle distance has increased slightly and the particles move around, though only within a limited space. (b) At the melting point the thermal energy is used to overcome the attractive forces; because even a slight increase in distance weakens the attraction drastically, the small increase lowers the attraction enough for the particles to leave their fixed positions.
s: (a) close and vibrating below; slightly farther apart and moving within a limited space after melting
(b) thermal energy overcomes attraction; slight extra distance weakens it enough

questions.q:
Compare and analyse the spreading of potassium permanganate colour through water and of an incense fragrance through the air of a room.
(a) In each case, name which particles are spreading and which particles are hitting them. (1)
(b) Explain what single property of the hitting particles makes both kinds of spreading happen. (1)
(c) For the water, describe the extra step that happens before the colour can spread, which the incense smoke does not need. (1)
(d) In which of the two cases can the hitting particles move through all the available space, and in which only within a limited space? (1)
(e) Explain why no such spreading happens through the inside of a solid block at room temperature. (1)
questions.a: (a) Water: potassium permanganate particles spread, hit by water particles. Room: fragrance particles spread, hit by air particles. (b) The hitting particles (water particles and air particles) are in constant motion. (c) The water particles first have to pull the potassium permanganate particles out of the solid grain before they can spread them. (d) Air particles (a gas) move through all the available space, so the fragrance can fill the room; water particles (a liquid) move only within a limited space, so the colour spreads through the water in the tumbler. (e) In a solid the particles are held in fixed positions by strong attraction and can only vibrate (movement negligible), so they cannot move through the block and carry other particles along.
s: (a) spreading and hitting particles named for both
(b) constant motion of water and air particles
(c) water particles first pull particles out of the grain
(d) air particles through all the space; water particles within a limited space
(e) solid particles only vibrate in fixed positions

questions.q: True or false? 'The fragrance of an incense stick lit in a corner would still spread through the whole of a closed room even if every fan were off and no window were open.' Give your verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The spreading does not need a wind or a fan. The particles of air are always moving; they keep hitting the particles of the fragrance and help them spread throughout the room, so the fragrance is felt first near the stick and soon everywhere.
s: verdict: true
constantly moving air particles hit the fragrance particles and spread them without any fan

questions.q: Describe one everyday solid (not sand, stone or potassium permanganate) that colours or flavours still water on its own, and one that, like sand, does not dissolve in water. Use the chapter's account of what moving water particles do to explain the difference.
questions.a: Any valid pair, for example: a sugar cube or a lump of salt left in still water slowly flavours all of it, while a glass marble or a steel spoon left in water does not dissolve. Explanation: the water particles are in constant motion; for the soluble solid they pull its particles out and then hit them so that they spread through the water. In the insoluble solid the constituent particles are held together so strongly that the water particles are unable to pull them out, so nothing spreads.
s: a valid soluble solid and a valid insoluble solid
moving water particles pull particles out of the soluble solid and spread them
the insoluble solid's particles are held too strongly to be pulled out
